text: Why does the air from a vent hug the ceiling? Let's follow it from the blower.
A spinning blower wheel flings air outward, building a pressure difference of about half an inch of water. Tiny, but enough to push air through the house.
In the main duct, air moves about nine hundred feet per minute. Where the duct narrows, it speeds up. Where it widens, it slows, and pressure climbs back.
Friction, and every elbow, costs pressure. Branch ducts run slower, about six hundred feet per minute.
At the diffuser, angled vanes fling the stream sideways, along the ceiling.
The fast jet drags air out of the gap above it. Pressure drops there, and the jet gets pulled onto the ceiling. That's the Coanda effect.
Then it breaks into turbulent eddies, mixing and slowing. Engineers size it to drop below fifty feet per minute by the end of its throw.
By the time it reaches you, it's a gentle draft, under forty feet per minute. Warm air rises, cool air sinks.
That's why it hugs the ceiling: a fast jet, a low pressure gap, and a surface to cling to.

Congrats! You've discovered how air flows through a vent.
